slides.headline: This snake builds a nest. And eats snakes.
slides.sub: The strange family life of king cobras

slides.headline: A snake that eats snakes
slides.body: King cobras feed almost entirely on other snakes: rat snakes, pythons up to about 3 m, even venomous cobras, kraits and smaller king cobras.

slides.headline: She builds a nest
slides.body: Using a loop of her body like an arm, the female pulls dead leaves, soil and litter into a compact mound, then lays 20 to 50 eggs inside.

slides.headline: Then she stands guard
slides.body: She coils on or near the mound for about two months. Heat from the rotting leaves helps incubate the eggs, and the male may stay nearby.

slides.label: the longest king cobra ever confirmed
slides.body: King cobras are the world's largest venomous snakes, though most stay under 3.6 m. IUCN: Vulnerable (assessed 2011, as one species).

slides.headline: One king became four
slides.body: A 2024 revision split king cobras into four species. Northern and eastern India keeps Ophiophagus hannah; the Western Ghats has its own, O. kaalinga.
slides.source: Das et al., European Journal of Taxonomy (2024)

Britannica and Smithsonian's National Zoo: King cobra

caption:
King cobras (genus Ophiophagus) are snakes that build nests, and they eat almost nothing but other snakes.

The genus name fits: ophiophagous means snake-eating. Since 2024, scientists recognise four king cobra species, so the big snake of northern and eastern India is Ophiophagus hannah, while the Western Ghats king cobra is O. kaalinga. A king cobra's hiss is unusually low, closer to a growl, and in a threat display it can lift the front of its body about a metre off the ground.

Swipe for the nest, the menu and the split. Sources on the last slide.

Source: Das et al. (2024), European Journal of Taxonomy 961; Britannica; IUCN Red List.
